solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Some Plymouth gin knocked over nobleman

indicators.note: knocked over, the run of letters falls the other way, so it is read backwards
'some' of a phrase means only a part of its run of letters is wanted

parts.note: the letters running across the end of Plymouth, all of gin and the start of knocked

explanation.surface: Someone tipping over a bottle of Plymouth gin, a well-known English spirit, and drenching an aristocrat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Knocked over' reads as one phrase about the gin, but 'knocked' supplies a letter and only 'over' does the turning.
explanation.definitionFit: A knight holds a title conferred by the monarch, so he counts loosely as a member of the titled nobility.

clue.text: Josh has new revolutionary 19

indicators.note: a word that has something holds it inside itself

parts.note: to josh is to tease, as is to kid
N is the standard abbreviation for new
a Red is a communist revolutionary

explanation.surface: Someone joking that a new rebel figure shares an affinity with tribal ways.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is a cross-reference: 19 points to the answer at 19-down, TRIBAL, which is the meaning to find.
explanation.definitionFit: Kindred describes people bound by blood or common ancestry, just as tribal groups are united by shared descent.

clue.text: Old Peruvian food container with top removed

indicators.note: in a down entry the top is the first letter, which these words take away

parts.note: a tin can holds preserved food

explanation.surface: An archaeologist describing an ancient Andean food vessel whose lid has gone missing.
explanation.definitionFit: The Inca empire ruled ancient Peru, so one of its people is an Incan, an old Peruvian.

clue.text: The French name picked by proprietor is one from 18, say

indicators.note: something picked by another is held in its grasp, so it sits inside it

parts.note: a holder owns or possesses something, like a proprietor
la is French for the, feminine form
N is the abbreviation for name

explanation.surface: A shop owner choosing a French label for someone visiting from the Dutch port.
explanation.walkthrough: 18 points to 18-across, ROTTERDAM. That city is in the province of Holland, so its people are Hollanders; 'say' marks it as one example.
explanation.definitionFit: A Hollander is a native of Holland, and a person from Rotterdam, a city in that region, is one example.

clue.text: Small item of furniture is fixed

parts.note: S is the abbreviation for small, as on clothing labels
a table is a basic piece of furniture

explanation.surface: A furniture review pronouncing a little side table firm and wobble-free.
explanation.definitionFit: Something stable is firmly set and steady, not liable to move or change, which is what fixed means.

clue.text: Doctrine written up remains the same

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a principle or belief held by a group

definitions.note: a descriptive second definition: a word that, written upwards in a down entry, is unchanged, a palindrome
definitions.meaning: second meaning: a word that reads identically when its letters run from bottom to top

explanation.surface: A doctrine that, once committed to paper, stays unchanged forever.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests dogma set in stone; cryptically, 'written up' is reading a down entry upwards, and this word survives that unchanged.
explanation.definitionFit: A tenet is a principle or belief held as true by a church, school or movement, which is a doctrine.

clue.text: Gripped, bit and chewed bananas

indicators.note: bananas is slang for crazy, so the preceding letters go wild into a new order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A monkey seizing, biting and munching its way through some bananas.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bananas' looks like what was being eaten, but it is the anagram signal for 'bit' and 'chewed'.
explanation.definitionFit: To be gripped by something is to be held spellbound and enchanted by it, as if under a spell.

clue.text: Heads of executive note-taking company mislay pen

indicators.note: the heads of words are their first letters, one taken from each

parts.note: first letters of executive, note-taking and company
to mislay something is to lose it

explanation.surface: Office gossip: the bosses of a minute-taking firm keep misplacing their pens.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pen' looks like the writing instrument the note-takers would lose, but it is the verb meaning to shut in.
explanation.definitionFit: To pen animals is to shut them inside a fold or fence, which is to surround and confine them.

clue.text: Eritrea's marathon is in its capital? Quite the opposite!

indicators.note: with the sense flipped by the tail of the clue, the capital is in the words before it, sitting among their letters
this exclamation reverses the claim made before it, so what contains and what is contained swap places

parts.note: the letters spanning the end of Eritrea's and the start of marathon

explanation.surface: A question about whether a marathon in Eritrea is run through its capital city.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Quite the opposite!' turns the question round: the marathon is not in the capital, the capital is in 'Eritrea's marathon'. The answer is the capital of Eritrea.
explanation.definitionFit: Asmara is the seat of government and largest city of Eritrea, the country named in the clue, so it is its capital.

clue.text: Buffet comprised of joint and filled bread

parts.note: the knuckle is a finger joint
slices of bread with a filling
joins the two parts

explanation.surface: A buffet spread made up of joints of meat and filled rolls.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Buffet' looks like a cold spread, but here it is a blow; a knuckle sandwich is slang for a punch in the mouth.
explanation.definitionFit: To buffet is to strike, so a buffet is a blow, and a knuckle sandwich is a jocular name for a punch.

clue.text: Press club

definitions.meaning: first meaning: to smooth clothes with a heated appliance
second meaning: a golf club with an angled metal head

explanation.walkthrough: 'Press club' looks like a journalists' meeting place, but the words are two separate meanings.
explanation.definitionFit: You smooth creases out of shirts with a hot appliance of that name, and golfers carry a set of such numbered metal-headed clubs.

clue.text: Love's in other words being ready to make change

indicators.note: one thing being another means it is turned into it, so one piece is swapped for a different one

parts.note: adoration is deep love
or can mean in other words, as in 'the capital, or seat of power'
apt can mean ready or inclined, as in apt to learn

explanation.surface: A romantic willing, in other words, to alter themselves for their partner.
explanation.walkthrough: Love's 'in other words' being 'ready': the OR in ADORATION becomes APT. The 's is 'has', so Love has OR turned to APT.
explanation.definitionFit: An adaptation is an alteration made to suit new conditions, so it is a change, noun for noun.

clue.text: Heated, dry out?

indicators.note: out means disordered or put out of place, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A question about whether warming something is how to dry it.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is both the fodder with its signal and a description of the answer: heating something dries it out.
explanation.definitionFit: To dehydrate is to remove the water from something, often by heating it, which dries it out.

clue.text: Short moral discourse about detectives, one is out for blood

indicators.note: about means around, so one piece surrounds the others
something short is cut down, so the last letter goes

parts.note: a homily is a moralising sermon
the Criminal Investigation Department, the British police detective branch
a means one

explanation.surface: A brief sermon delivered to police officers about a killer on the loose.
explanation.walkthrough: CID, the Criminal Investigation Department, is the detective branch of British police forces.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone homicidal wants to kill, which is the idiom of being out for blood, eager to hurt or murder.

clue.text: That man in East London certainly had on women's make-up

parts.note: he said with a Cockney dropped H is 'e
certainly is an emphatic yes
taken as written
the letter O stands for on in some abbreviations
W is the abbreviation for women

explanation.surface: A Cockney saying that a man was definitely wearing a woman's cosmetics.
explanation.walkthrough: East London is Cockney territory, where the H of he is dropped. 'Had on' looks like wearing, but the words are separate pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: Eyeshadow is a coloured cosmetic applied to the eyelids, a standard part of a woman's make-up kit.

clue.text: Dog training command doctor voiced

indicators.note: voiced means spoken out, so the word is matched by its sound rather than its spelling

parts.note: to doctor a wound is to heal it

explanation.surface: A vet calling out commands while training a dog.
explanation.definitionFit: Owners order a dog to walk close beside their legs with this one-word instruction, a standard obedience call.

clue.text: Bathe in part of London with maiden

parts.note: SW1 is a central London postcode district, with the 1 read as the letter I
M is the cricket scorebook abbreviation for maiden over

explanation.surface: A girl taking a dip in some part of London.
explanation.walkthrough: SW1 is the postcode for Westminster and Belgravia; the digit 1 stands in for I.
explanation.definitionFit: To bathe can mean to go into the sea or a pool for a dip, which is to swim.

clue.text: Rich source of fluorine

parts.note: a well is a source of water
taken as written
F is the chemical symbol for fluorine

explanation.surface: A chemist describing a plentiful supply of fluorine.
explanation.definitionFit: Being comfortably prosperous with plenty of money is the idiom for having wealth, the same as rich.

clue.text: Rascal enthusiastic about European city

parts.note: a rotter is a cad or rascal

indicators.note: about can mean turned around, so the word is read backwards

parts.note: mad about something means very keen on it

explanation.surface: A scoundrel who just loves some continental city.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Enthusiastic about' looks like the phrase mad about, but 'about' here turns MAD around.
explanation.definitionFit: Rotterdam is a major port city in the Netherlands, so it is a city in Europe.

clue.text: Ethnic origin of Tony Blair disputed

indicators.note: something disputed is called into question and argued over, so the letters are thrown into a new order
the origin of a word is where it begins, its first letter

parts.note: first letter of Tony
taken as written

explanation.surface: A row over the ancestry of the former British Prime Minister Tony Blair.
explanation.definitionFit: Ethnic describes a group sharing common descent and culture, which is what tribal means.

clue.text: Reportedly crazed, chic model

indicators.note: something reported is passed on by speech, so the sound counts and not the spelling

parts.note: manic means crazed and in means fashionable or chic

explanation.surface: Gossip that a stylish fashion model has gone mad.
explanation.definitionFit: A manikin is a jointed figure used by artists or tailors, a dummy model of the human body.

clue.text: Artisan concocting kitsch balm

indicators.note: concocting means mixing up ingredients, so the letters are blended into something new

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A craftsman cooking up a tacky ointment.
explanation.definitionFit: A blacksmith is a skilled craftsman who forges iron by hand, one type of artisan.

clue.text: Extremely silly fellow upset group of clergymen

indicators.note: the extremes of a word are its two ends, the first and last letters

parts.note: the outer letters of silly

indicators.note: upset means knocked over, and in a down entry that turns the word upside down

parts.note: a don is a fellow of a university college

explanation.surface: A foolish man who has fallen out with the church council.
explanation.walkthrough: At Oxford and Cambridge a don is a college fellow.
explanation.definitionFit: A synod is an assembly of clergy, and sometimes laity, meeting to decide church matters.

clue.text: 'Ang out with female relative

indicators.note: the apostrophe in place of an H shows that a dropped H is to be dropped from the answer too

parts.note: to hang out somewhere is to frequent it, or haunt it

explanation.surface: A Cockney inviting someone to spend time with a female family member.
explanation.walkthrough: The Cockney 'ang for hang tells you to drop the H from the synonym too, leaving 'AUNT.
explanation.definitionFit: An aunt is the sister of one's parent, so she is a woman in the family, a female relation.

clue.text: Ace detective died arresting hard little sucker

parts.note: A is the abbreviation for ace on playing cards

indicators.note: arresting someone means seizing and holding them, so one piece is held inside

parts.note: a PI is a private investigator
H stands for hard, as on pencils
D is the abbreviation for died, as in genealogies

explanation.surface: A star sleuth dies while catching a tough little crook.
explanation.walkthrough: PI and D together hold H: A + P(H)I + D.
explanation.definitionFit: Aphids are tiny insects that feed by piercing plants and drawing out sap, so they are small suckers.

clue.text: Group of former workers fish — this may be hoped for on retirement!

definitions.text: this may be hoped for on retirement

parts.note: G stands for group, as in G7 or G20
olden means of former times
hands are manual workers, as in farmhands
a hake is a sea fish of the cod family

explanation.surface: A reunion of ex-employees going fishing, each hoping for a generous send-off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Group of former workers' reads like retired staff, but each word is a separate piece; G is the group of G7 and G20.
explanation.definitionFit: A golden handshake is a large payment given to a departing employee, the kind of lump sum people hope to receive when leaving work.

clue.text: 10:50, I go with daughter and son to see Cats

parts.note: 10-across is IRON, whose chemical symbol is Fe
L is the Roman numeral for fifty
taken as written
D is the abbreviation for daughter
S is the abbreviation for son

explanation.surface: A parent taking their children to the 10:50 performance of the musical Cats.
explanation.walkthrough: '10:50' looks like a showtime, but 10 points to 10-across, iron, and 50 is a Roman numeral. Cats is the long-running Lloyd Webber musical.
explanation.definitionFit: Felids are members of the biological family Felidae, which takes in all wild and domestic cats.

clue.text: Journalist in news broadcast in European country

indicators.note: one piece placed in another sits inside it
broadcast means scattered widely, as seed is, so these letters are strewn into a new order

parts.note: taken as written
ED is short for editor, the journalist in charge

explanation.surface: A reporter appearing on a television news bulletin from Scandinavia.
explanation.definitionFit: Sweden is a Scandinavian nation in northern Europe, so it is one of the countries of that continent.
